stem: A company stores application logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each log file is larger than 1 MB, and the bucket holds the only copy. Engineers read the logs often for 30 days and rarely from day 30 to day 90, when a log must still open in milliseconds. After 90 days, the logs are an archive: auditors read a few logs each year and can wait up to 24 hours for a log. The company must retain the logs for 7 years and then delete them. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

options.text: Add one lifecycle rule that transitions the logs to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days, and moves a log back to S3 Standard when an auditor asks for it.
options.why: A lifecycle transition [can go only one way](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-no-transition-out-of-archive), so no rule moves a log from Deep Archive back to S3 Standard.

options.text: Add one lifecycle rule that transitions the logs to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days, and expires them after 7 years.
options.why: Standard-IA keeps logs [available for millisecond access](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-classes-millisecond-access-retrieval-fee) until day 90, and Deep Archive returns data [within 12 hours](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-times-deep) with a Standard retrieval, well inside the 24 hours of the auditors.

options.text: Add one lifecycle rule that transitions the logs to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and to S3 One Zone-IA after 90 days, and expires them after 7 years.
options.why: S3 One Zone-IA is [not resilient to the physical loss](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use) of its zone, and the bucket holds the only copy of the logs.

options.text: Add one lifecycle rule that transitions the logs to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days, and expires them after 7 years.
options.why: It works, but S3 Glacier Deep Archive is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours) and still meets the wait of the auditors.

explanation: Each storage class matches one stage of the logs. Standard-IA serves the rare reads that need milliseconds. From day 90, S3 Glacier Deep Archive is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours), and a Standard retrieval finishes [within 12 hours](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-times-deep), which fits the wait of the auditors. The rule follows [a waterfall model for transitioning between storage classes](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-transition-waterfall) and then expires the logs.
takeaway: Build a lifecycle rule from the access pattern: an IA class for rare fast reads, then the coldest class that meets the wait.
twin: If the stem said "auditors need a log within 5 hours" instead: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days, because a Standard retrieval there takes [3–5 hours](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-times-flexible).
say: Standard-IA for the rare fast reads, Deep Archive after day ninety, and expire at seven years.

solvers.stem_only: One lifecycle rule: S3 Standard for 30 days, transition to S3 Standard-IA at day 30 (multi-AZ, ms access), transition to S3 Glacier Deep Archive at day 90 (standard retrieval within 12 hours), expire after 7 years.

solvers.flag: The stem names no retrieval tier, so a candidate could defend S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval over Deep Archive because a 12-hour wait leaves no margin for Deep Archive standard retrieval.
